fixes.explanation: John 18:2 says Judas, His betrayer, knew the place because Jesus had often met there with His disciples. That's the reason the text gives. Then in verse 3 Judas brings the soldiers and officers to the garden. I think that stings a little extra.

Nope, the text doesn't say the chief priests showed him anything. John 18:2 gives the reason: Judas knew the place because Jesus had often met there with His disciples. The verse names no guide at all.
That one's not in the text, friend. John 18:2 gives the reason: Jesus had often met there with His disciples. Land and family aren't mentioned in that verse. That's the only reason it gives.

John 18:3 says Judas brought a band of soldiers and officers from the chief priests and Pharisees. So the officers came from the chief priests and Pharisees. They arrived at the garden carrying lanterns, torches, and weapons. That's quite a crowd.

Yes, John 18:3 says they arrived carrying lanterns, torches, and weapons. That's not a casual walk in the garden. They came with light and they came ready. Think of someone showing up to pick up one cookie box with a whole moving crew.
John 18:3 says they arrived carrying lanterns, torches, and weapons. So the weapons sit right in the verse, next to the lights. Lanterns AND torches AND weapons? That's a lot of full hands, friend.

John 18:4 says Jesus, knowing all that was coming upon Him, stepped forward and asked, "Whom are you seeking?" He doesn't run and He doesn't hide. He steps forward. I'll be honest, I once hid from a smoke alarm. This is a different level.
Jesus says the opposite. In John 18:8 He says, "So if you are looking for Me, let these men go." He speaks up for the men with Him. Taking them along isn't in His request.

That's not what He says. John 18:8 has Jesus say, "So if you are looking for Me, let these men go." There's no questioning in His words, just the request to let the men go. I think His disciples are on His mind, and He says so with all those torches in front of Him.

The writer says it fulfills the word Jesus had spoken: "I have not lost one of those You have given Me." (John 18:9) The writer connects that word to Jesus speaking up for His disciples in the garden. Not one of them lost. That's a word with some weight to it.

Not quite. In John 18:11 Jesus says, "Put your sword back in its sheath!" He tells Peter to put it away, not to stand his ground. Peter's swing had already cut off the right ear of the high priest's servant, Malchus (John 18:10). I think this part of the story is a heavy one.

Jesus says, "Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?" (John 18:11) The cup is something the Father has given Him. Jesus asks it as a question, and He asks it right after telling Peter to put his sword back. So the word that fills the blank is Father.

The high priest is named in this passage, as the one Malchus serves (John 18:10). But the cup isn't from him. Jesus says, "Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?" (John 18:11). The cup comes from the Father.
